title: Kautsa and the rain of gold
hook: a student owes his teacher fourteen crore gold coins, and goes to a king who has nothing left
carry: gurudakshina: learning ends with a gift to the teacher
tomorrow: what does the greatest archer alive do when he's lost?

segments.voice: Yesterday gave two send-offs, live in the world or go the day it calls: the ashramas honor both home and going forth. Today, the gift that closes a student's years.

A young man named Kautsa has just finished years of study in his teacher's house. Before he goes home, he begs to give his teacher something. The teacher, Varatantu, says his devotion is enough. Kautsa keeps insisting. Finally the teacher, annoyed, names a price: you learned fourteen branches of knowledge, so bring fourteen crore gold coins. Kautsa has nothing. So he walks to the most generous king alive, and the king greets him holding a clay pot.
screen: `A STUDENT INSISTS.` → `FOURTEEN CRORE GOLD COINS.` → `A KING WITH A CLAY POT.`

segments.voice: The king is Raghu, the ancestor of Rama, and the story is told by the poet Kalidasa. Raghu has just given away everything he owned in a great sacrifice; that's why he serves his guest from clay instead of gold. Kautsa sees it and turns to leave: he won't ask a king who has nothing. Raghu stops him. No student who came to him for his teacher's sake will go away empty-handed. Stay a few days, he says. Raghu makes up his mind to march on Kubera, the god of wealth, himself. Before he sets out, gold rains down into his empty treasury. Raghu offers Kautsa all of it. Kautsa takes only the fourteen crore he owes, not a coin more, and the city praises them both: a student who wanted no more than his due, and a king who gave more than he was asked. Here's the teaching. It's called gurudakshina, the gift to the guru, and the old law books place it right at the end of study, before the graduate's bath, the samavartana that sends him home. Yesterday's Taittiriya said it too: bring your teacher a gift. In this tradition knowledge isn't bought. It's received, and the gift afterward is thanks, not payment. The same word, dakshina, names the gift families still hand the pandit after a puja, and students still honor their teachers on Guru Purnima. And a teacher isn't only someone in a classroom: that same Upanishad says, let your mother be a god to you, your father, your teacher.
screen: `RAGHU GAVE EVERYTHING AWAY.` · `GOLD RAINS DOWN.` · `ONLY WHAT HE OWED.` · `GURUDAKSHINA: THANKS, NOT PAYMENT.`

segments.voice: Pour a little water into a cup, the way the graduate's bath began his walk home. Dip your fingertips in and touch them to your eyelids; notice the cool. Then hold the cup in both hands and name, silently, one teacher you never properly thanked. If you pray, offer the water and the name together, the way an offering is made at a puja. If you don't, just hold the cup and the name until the cool fades. Then, today, send that person a few words of thanks: your own small dakshina.
The graduate's path: the gift, then the bath and the walk home. Gurudakshina is thanks, not payment.
For the road: gurudakshina, learning ends with a gift to the teacher. Kautsa took only what he owed.

howItsDone: Families give dakshina to the priest after a puja or a life rite, and many students honor their teachers with a gift or a bow on Guru Purnima; Kautsa's story is retold from Kalidasa's Raghuvamsha.

chat.meaning: Gurudakshina is the student's thank-you when the learning is done, like Kautsa's for Varatantu. It's thanks, not payment, and the Taittiriya counts your mother and father among your teachers, so a grandmother who taught you counts too.

Kautsa.meaning: a student who insisted on giving his teacher a gift

Raghu.meaning: a generous king, ancestor of Rama

gurudakshina.meaning: the gift to the guru when study is done

samavartana.meaning: the returning home: the rite that ends a student's years

snataka.meaning: a graduate; tradition reads it as one who has bathed

sources.ref: Kalidasa, Raghuvamsha, canto 5 (Kautsa, pupil of Varatantu, presses his teacher to name a gift and is asked fourteen crores for the fourteen branches of learning; Raghu, having given all away in the Vishvajit sacrifice, receives him with an earthen vessel; Raghu resolves to march on Kubera; gold rains into the treasury; Kautsa takes only what is owed; the people praise both)
Manusmriti 2.245–246 (the student gives nothing to the teacher beforehand; when about to bathe at the end of study, with the teacher's leave, he brings a gift as he is able)
Paraskara Grihya Sutra 2.6 (the samavartana: having finished the Veda, let him bathe)
Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11.1–2 (bring the teacher a gift; let your mother, father and teacher be as gods to you; yesterday's parting words, recalled)
